Fix null-pointer crash in login handler

The handler read `session.user_id` before checking whether the session
lookup actually returned a row. Any login with an expired or unknown
token dereferenced nil and crashed the request instead of returning 401.

Check the lookup result first and return 401 on a miss. Adds a test for
the expired-token path, which is how this shipped uncaught.

# Add rate limiting to the API

## What

Per-client rate limiting on all `/api/*` routes, enforced in middleware before the handler runs.

- **Limits**: 100 req/min per API key, 20 req/min per IP for unauthenticated requests.
- **Algorithm**: sliding window counter in Redis, keyed `ratelimit:{client}:{window}`.
- **Response**: `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After`, plus `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset` on every response, not only on rejections, so clients can back off before they get cut off.

## Why

One integration burst on us last week and pushed p99 past 4s for everyone else on the shared pool. Nothing in front of the handlers stops that today.

## Testing

Verified: unit tests cover the boundary (request 100 passes, 101 gets `429`) and window rollover across the minute edge. Load test locally at 500 rps against one instance, limiter added ~0.4ms p50.

Assumed, not verified: behavior under real Redis failure. There's a unit test for the fail-open path with a mocked client, but I haven't pulled Redis out from under a running instance. Worth a second set of eyes there.

## Rollout

Ships behind `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED`, default off. Staging for a week, watch the `429` rate by client, then production. If Redis is unreachable the limiter fails open and logs, so a Redis outage degrades to current behavior rather than dropping traffic. That's a deliberate call: I'd rather serve an unlimited burst than reject everyone during an outage. Flip it if you disagree, it's one constant.

Start with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the exact query with the exact parameter values. Everything else is guessing until you see the plan.

What you're looking for, in order:

- **Did the plan change?** A sequential scan where you expect an index scan is the usual answer. Compare `rows` (estimated) against `actual rows` in the output. If the estimate is off by 100x, the planner is working from stale statistics.
- **Stale stats.** Run `ANALYZE your_table;` and re-run the query. If it gets fast, autovacuum is falling behind. Check `SELECT relname, last_autoanalyze, last_autovacuum, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'your_table';`
- **Bloat.** Lots of dead tuples means the same logical rows cost more pages to read. `n_dead_tup` relative to `n_live_tup` tells you.
- **Data crossed a threshold.** A table that grew past the point where the planner prefers a seq scan will flip plans overnight with no code change. Same query, same index, different decision.
- **Locks.** If the query is waiting rather than working, `pg_stat_activity` shows `wait_event_type` and `wait_event`. 20 seconds of blocking looks identical to 20 seconds of scanning from the outside.

My bet before seeing anything: stale statistics or a plan flip from data growth, since "fine last week, terrible now" with unchanged code points at the planner rather than the query.

One thing to rule out early: confirm the query itself is actually slow, and it isn't a connection pool exhausted upstream making every query look slow. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` from `psql` settles that in one shot.

REST. Small team, mobile client, no strong pull toward GraphQL in what you described.

The case for REST here:

- **Less to operate.** No schema server, no resolver layer, no N+1 analysis, no query cost limiting. GraphQL's operational surface is real work that a small team pays for continuously.
- **Caching is free.** HTTP caching, CDN, `ETag`, conditional requests all work out of the box. In GraphQL every read is a `POST` to one endpoint, so you rebuild caching yourself or add a client library that does it.
- **Debugging is a `curl` away.** Matters more than it sounds when you're chasing a mobile bug from a crash report.

The real case for GraphQL, so you can check whether it applies to you:

- **Many clients with divergent data needs**, especially several mobile versions live at once that you can't force to update. GraphQL lets an old client keep asking for the fields it knows about while the schema grows.
- **Deeply nested reads** where REST would mean five round trips on a bad cell connection.
- **A dedicated backend team** that will own the schema and the performance work.

If you're one team shipping one app, the first two problems are solvable with a couple of purpose-built endpoints that return exactly what a screen needs. That's cheaper than a query language.

The call I'd make: REST, and if you find yourself writing `?include=` and `?fields=` parameters everywhere to satisfy different screens, that's your signal to revisit. Reaching that point takes most teams a long time, and some never do.

An index is a separate sorted data structure that maps column values to row locations, so the database can jump to the rows it wants instead of reading every row and checking. Same idea as the index in the back of a book.

Concretely, in Postgres a B-tree index on `users(email)` turns `WHERE email = 'x@y.com'` from a scan of every row into a handful of page reads down a tree. On a million-row table that's the difference between hundreds of milliseconds and under a millisecond.

Where it hurts:

- **Every write pays.** `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` must update the index too. Five indexes on a table means five extra structures maintained per write. On write-heavy tables this is the main cost.
- **Storage and memory.** Indexes take real disk, and they compete with your table data for the buffer cache. An index nobody uses is evicting pages somebody does.
- **Low-cardinality columns are usually pointless.** An index on a boolean `is_active` where 90% of rows are `true` doesn't help, because reading 90% of the table through an index is slower than just scanning it. The planner will often ignore it, and you'll have paid the write cost for nothing.
- **Small tables don't need them.** Under a few thousand rows, a sequential scan is frequently faster than the index lookup plus heap fetch.
- **Redundant indexes.** An index on `(a, b)` already serves queries filtering on `a` alone. A separate index on `(a)` is pure overhead. This one is common and easy to miss.

The practical rule: add indexes in response to a slow query you can point at, not in anticipation. Then check `pg_stat_user_indexes` a few weeks later and drop the ones with `idx_scan = 0`, they're costing you writes and buying nothing.

Probably not worth it unless you have a specific pain Jira is causing, and you can name it. "Linear is nicer" is true and usually not enough to justify a migration.

What actually decides this:

- **Where your pain is.** If it's speed and UI friction, Linear wins clearly and people will feel it daily. If it's process (approvals, compliance, custom workflows per team, portfolio-level reporting), Linear is deliberately more opinionated and you'll be fighting it inside six months.
- **Team size and shape.** Linear fits product engineering teams well. If support, legal, IT, or marketing also live in your Jira, they mostly don't have a home in Linear, and you end up with two tools plus the seam between them.
- **The Atlassian gravity.** Confluence, Bitbucket, and Jira Service Management links all break or degrade. Check how much of your documentation links into Jira issues before you decide.
- **Migration cost, honestly counted.** The importer moves issues, comments, and basic fields. It does not cleanly move custom fields, complex workflows, automation rules, dashboards, or historical reporting. Budget a real week for someone, plus a few weeks of everyone being slightly lost.
- **History.** Old issues come across as data, but your saved filters, boards, and any tooling reading the Jira API are yours to rewrite.

What I'd do: run one team on Linear for a full quarter, in parallel, with real work. Not a trial project, actual sprints. At the end, ask that team whether they'd go back. That answer is worth more than any comparison table, and it costs you one team's ramp-up instead of the whole org's.

One caveat I'd keep in front of you: tool migrations feel productive and often aren't. If the underlying problem is that tickets are vague and priorities change weekly, Linear will render that problem in a faster interface.

Split the 60% by where they stop before you theorize about why. One number covering "signup to first action" is hiding at least three different failure modes with different fixes.

Steps, in the order that pays off fastest:

- **Instrument the intermediate steps.** Email verification sent, verification clicked, first screen loaded, first screen interacted with, action completed. If your analytics can't tell those apart today, that's step zero and everything else waits on it.
- **Segment the drop.** By platform (mobile web is usually the worst), by acquisition channel (paid traffic converts differently from organic and it's often not a product problem at all), by whether they arrived with an invite, and by time-to-first-action. A drop concentrated in one segment is a much easier problem than a uniform one.
- **Check the boring failures first.** Verification emails landing in spam, an OAuth redirect broken on one browser, a required field that rejects valid input, a 4MB first screen on a 3G connection. These account for a startling share of funnel drops and cost nothing to check.
- **Watch ten session recordings** of users who dropped. Ten is enough to see a pattern. This is the single highest-information-per-hour thing on the list, and it usually contradicts whatever the team assumed.
- **Then talk to five people who dropped.** Ask what they were trying to do and what they expected to happen. Not whether they liked it.

Two things that will mislead you if you skip them. First, some of that 60% are bots and never-serious signups, especially on a free tier, so establish your real denominator before you set a target. Second, "first action" may be the wrong action to measure. If it's something a user reasonably wouldn't do on day one, the funnel is fine and the metric is wrong.

I'd start with instrumentation plus the ten recordings, in parallel. You'll likely have a hypothesis by the end of the week.

Give the feedback plainly and early in the conversation, then spend the time on what changes. Demoralizing usually comes from ambiguity and surprise, not from directness.

What works:

- **One issue, not a list.** Three pieces of critical feedback in one sitting reads as an indictment and none of them land. Pick the one that matters most.
- **Behavior and effect, not character.** "The last three specs shipped without the migration plan, and the on-call engineer found out at deploy time" is actionable. "You're careless" is not, and it can't be fixed.
- **Say it in the first minute.** Leading with praise so the criticism has a cushion trains them to hear compliments as a warning siren. It also means they spend the whole conversation waiting for it.
- **Ask before you conclude.** They may have context you don't. "What's getting in the way here?" costs one minute and occasionally reveals that the problem is a process, or you.
- **Be explicit about the stakes.** If this is a small correction, say that. If it's genuinely affecting their standing, say that too. People fill silence with the worst interpretation, and someone who thinks a minor note is a firing warning is far more demoralized than someone told the truth.
- **Leave with a specific next step and a date.** "Bring me the migration plan with the next spec, and let's check in in two weeks."

The part people skip: follow up when it improves. Feedback that only ever arrives when something is wrong teaches them that a meeting with you means bad news, and that's the thing that actually corrodes morale over a year.

If they get defensive in the room, don't argue and don't retreat from the point. "I hear you, and I still need the migration plan attached going forward. Let's talk again Thursday once you've sat with it." Retracting under pressure is the one move that guarantees you'll have this conversation again.

`502 Bad Gateway` means the server you reached was acting as a proxy or gateway, and the upstream server it forwarded your request to returned an invalid response, or nothing at all.

The failure is behind the proxy, not in your request. Retrying is reasonable, since the common causes are transient: an upstream process that crashed, a backend still booting, or a connection refused or reset mid-response.

Its neighbor `504 Gateway Timeout` is the case where the upstream accepted the connection and then never answered in time. If you're debugging your own stack, the useful logs are the upstream service's. The proxy only knows it got garbage back.

A race condition is when two pieces of code touch the same data at the same time, and the result depends on which one happens to get there first. Run it a thousand times and you get the right answer nine hundred and ninety times, which is the part that makes it painful.

The classic example. Two threads both run `counter = counter + 1` on a counter currently at `5`. That single line is really three operations: read the value, add one, write it back. Interleave them badly:

```
Thread A reads counter -> 5
Thread B reads counter -> 5
Thread A computes 5 + 1, writes 6
Thread B computes 5 + 1, writes 6
```

Two increments happened. The counter says `6`. It should say `7`.

Nothing in your single-threaded intuition prepares you for this, because in single-threaded code a line finishes before the next one starts. With concurrency that guarantee is gone. Any instruction can be interrupted partway through by another thread doing the same work on the same memory.

What makes them nasty in practice:

- **They're timing-dependent**, so they show up under production load and vanish in your debugger, since attaching a debugger changes the timing.
- **A test that passes proves nothing.** It proves that on that run the interleaving was benign.
- **The corruption is silent.** No exception, no crash, just a number that's quietly wrong, or two users assigned the same order ID.

The fix is to make the read-modify-write sequence indivisible, so no other thread can observe or interfere with the middle of it. That's what a mutex, an atomic operation, or a database transaction each do in their own domain.

You can hit this without threads, too. Two HTTP requests reading a row, both deciding a seat is available, and both booking it is the exact same bug with a database standing in for shared memory.
